sections.heading: What is String / Sequence DP?
sections.content: This family of DP problems works on one or two sequences (strings or arrays) and asks for the longest, shortest, cheapest or number of ways to match, transform or select parts of them. The most common state is dp[i][j]: the answer for the first i characters of string A and the first j characters of string B. Each cell is built from three neighbors: the diagonal (both characters used), the cell above (skip a character of A) and the cell to the left (skip a character of B). The core problems are Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), Edit Distance, Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) and their many variants.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Compare two strings: longest common subsequence, edit distance, interleaving, matching with wildcards
Find the longest increasing, palindromic or chain-like subsequence in one sequence
Count the ways one string can be formed from another (distinct subsequences)
Convert one string into another with the fewest operations
Questions about deleting, inserting or replacing characters
Keywords: subsequence, common, edit distance, delete, insert, replace, match, interleave, palindromic subsequence, increasing

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Imagine laying the two strings along the edges of a grid, one down the left and one across the top. Cell (i, j) answers the question for the prefixes A[0 until i] and B[0 until j]. When the last characters of the two prefixes match, you can pair them and build on cell (i - 1, j - 1). When they do not match, one of them has to be left out, so you take the better of dropping the last character of A (cell above) or of B (cell to the left). Filling the grid row by row builds the full answer from tiny prefixes.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Mixing up the dp index (first i characters) and the string index (a[i - 1] for dp row i)
Forgetting the base cases for the empty prefixes (row 0 and column 0)
Resetting to 0 on mismatch in a subsequence problem, or carrying over in a substring problem
Computing max and min with the wrong neighbors in Edit Distance (replace uses the diagonal)
Sorting heights ascending for equal widths in Russian Doll Envelopes
Using the O(n log n) LIS tails array as if it were the actual subsequence
Using strict < for a non-decreasing subsequence, which needs <=
Space-optimizing before confirming correctness, then losing the ability to rebuild the answer
Int overflow when counting subsequences (use Long or a modulo if the problem says so)

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Two-string DP uses dp[i][j] over prefixes, built from the diagonal, up and left neighbors
On a match LCS extends the diagonal, and on a mismatch it takes the better of up or left
Substring problems reset to 0 on a mismatch, while subsequence problems carry the best neighbor
Edit Distance adds 1 for replace, delete or insert and takes the minimum of the three
Many problems reduce to LCS: delete distance, supersequence, palindromic subsequence
LIS is O(n²) with DP and O(n log n) with a tails array and binary search
